A graph has degeneracy >= 2 iff it contains a cycle, so the cycle-in-out-neighbourhood statement is exactly the d=2 instance of the degeneracy question; the authors present it as such.

source.name: High chromatic number forcing high degeneracy out-neighbourhood
source.statement: Does there exist, for each integer $d$, an integer $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\geqslant\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, there is a vertex $v$ for which $G[N^{+}_{T}(v)]$ has degeneracy at least $d$?
source.context: In the closing remarks the authors note they have been unable to determine whether high chromatic number forces an out-neighbourhood with high degeneracy. The paper's disproof of Conjecture 1 shows chromatic number is not preserved, but degeneracy is a weaker measure and may behave differently.

target.name: Cycle in out-neighbourhood for high-χ graphs
target.statement: For every graph $G$ with sufficiently large chromatic number, and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, there exists a vertex $v$ such that $G[N^{+}_{T}(v)]$ contains a cycle.
target.context: The authors suspect that the case $d=2$ of Question 10 is true, i.e., high chromatic number should force some out-neighbourhood to contain a cycle. This is the weakest non-trivial instance of the degeneracy question, since bipartite graphs (which arise in their counterexamples) are acyclic-free but 1-degenerate.

sketches: Both records ask whether 4-colorability of graphs embedded in a fixed surface (other than the sphere) can be decided in polynomial time.

Both ask whether 4-colorability of graphs embedded in a fixed surface can be tested in polynomial time; the sphere case is trivial by the Four Color Theorem, so 'fixed surface' and 'fixed surface other than the sphere' state the same open problem.

source.name: 4-colorability on fixed surfaces complexity
source.statement: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm for testing 4-colorability of graphs drawn in $\Sigma$ when $\Sigma$ is a fixed surface other than the sphere?
source.context: The authors note that while 5-colorability on any fixed surface can be decided in polynomial (even linear) time using the finiteness of 6-critical graphs (Theorem 1), the analogous question for 4-colorability is open, and the techniques currently available do not give much hope for a positive resolution in the near future.

target.name: Polynomial-time 4-colorability on fixed surfaces
target.statement: Whether 4-colorability of graphs embedded in a fixed surface can be tested in polynomial time remains open; the authors remark that prospects for its resolution in the near future are not very bright.
target.context: After announcing that Theorem 1.3 completes one of two missing steps in Thomassen's polynomial-time colorability program, the authors identify the remaining open step as the analogous question for 4-coloring graphs on a fixed surface.

Both pose the open complexity of 3-colourability on P_t-free graphs (known polytime for t ≤ 7): one asks to determine the complexity for t ≥ 8, the other asks whether it is polynomial for every fixed t; the open content is identical.

Both ask the complexity of 3-colourability on P_t-free graphs for large t: 1803.05396__00 asks to determine it for t >= 8 (smaller t known polynomial), 1806.11196__00 conjectures polynomial for every fixed t; the open content is identical.

source.name: 3-colourability complexity of P_t-free graphs
source.statement: Determine the complexity of $3$-colourability of $P_t$-free graphs for $t \geq 8$.
source.context: Polynomial-time algorithms for 3-colourability of $P_t$-free graphs are known for $t \leq 7$ (combining results for $t \leq 5$, $(k,t)=(3,7)$, and hardness for $P_7$-free graphs). The paper notes this problem remains open for $t \geq 8$, and provides a subexponential-time algorithm as partial progress.

target.name: Polynomial 3-coloring for P_t-free graphs
target.statement: Is it true that for every (fixed) integer $t > 0$, the 3-coloring problem can be solved in polynomial time when restricted to the class of $P_t$-free graphs?
target.context: Theorem 1.1 (from the literature) states that if the $k$-coloring problem is polynomial on $H$-free graphs then every connected component of $H$ must be a path. For $k=3$ the converse may hold — it is known to fail for $k>4$ — so the question of whether $P_t$-free graphs always admit a polynomial-time 3-coloring algorithm remains open. The present paper contributes a positive result for the subclass of $(P_6+rP_3)$-free graphs.

sketches: A path P_t is a linear forest with one component; polynomial-time 3-Coloring on H-free graphs for every H whose components are paths restricts, at H=P_t, to polynomial-time 3-coloring of P_t-free graphs.

P_t is a graph all of whose components are paths, so 'if every component of H is a path then 3-Coloring on H-free graphs is polytime' yields, for H=P_t, a polynomial-time 3-coloring algorithm on P_t-free graphs for every t.
A single path P_t is a linear forest (every component a path), so polynomial 3-Coloring on H-free graphs for all path-component H restricted to H = P_t gives exactly the P_t-free 3-coloring question.

source.name: Polynomial 3-coloring for path-component-free graphs
source.statement: If every component of $H$ is a path, then the $3$-Coloring Problem restricted to $H$-free graphs can be solved in polynomial time.
source.context: Theorem 1.1 (Holyer; Kamiński and Lozin) establishes that if $H$ has at least one component which is not a path then the $3$-Coloring Problem on $H$-free graphs is NP-hard. Immediately after stating this theorem the paper notes: 'The converse to Theorem 1.1 is wide open.'
